pages.title: Teacher's Guide to This Course
pages.html:
Teacher's Guide to This Course

Course shape

Mississippi History, grades 9-12, Mississippi Studies standards. This portion of the course is Modules 19-36: Quarter 3 (Modules 19-27, Civil War and Reconstruction through the Great Flood and the Depression years) and Quarter 4 (Modules 28-36, Civil Rights, modern Mississippi, government, the economy, newcomers, and the arts). Each module has two lessons, two primary sources, a discussion, and one assignment.

What is in each module (in order)

  1. Intro Wrapper (survey quiz; includes the Module Map)
  2. Lessons N.1 and N.2
  3. Primary Source N.1 and N.2 pages
  4. Primary Source Exercises (4 questions each)
  5. Discussion
  6. Module Assignment: Reading Quiz, VR Activity, or Primary Source Report, per the course map
  7. Outro Wrapper (survey quiz)

Grading groups

GroupWeightHolds
Asynchronous Homework60%Primary Source Exercises, Reading Quizzes, VR Activities, Primary Source Reports
Projects30%Quarter 3 Exam and Quarter 4 Exam (30% of the semester by default; adjust in Canvas if you prefer)
Synchronous Homework & Activities10%18 module discussions
Teacher-Facing (ungraded)0%Semester Final

Point values are placeholders until the course wrap-up; the group weights are already in force.

Where your time goes

Most items are auto-graded. Your hands-on grading is the Discussion (rubric, read in batches) and the Primary Source Report or VR Activity in the modules that have one. The wrapper surveys give you cohort-level confidence ratings and "what is unclear" responses to scan at the start of each module cycle.

Quarter exams and the Semester Final

Each quarter exam is multiple choice and covers that quarter only (about 30 questions). The Semester Final (about 58 questions) is for your use and draws from both quarters.

Lesson pages: audio support

Every lesson and primary-source page has a Listen player at the top that reads the page aloud with the browser's built-in voice. Each glossary entry also has a speaker button that says the word. Voices vary by device and browser.

Not yet final

  • Primary Source pages are drafts; scans or verified text are still being inserted.
  • Several primary sources are not yet chosen (21.2, 27.1, 29.2, 31.2, 33.2, 34.1, 34.2, 36.2).
  • VR Activities need session details before they can be assigned.
  • Point values, attempts, and dates are not set.

Benchmarks: Standards Index (teacher-facing)

Mississippi Studies (MDE), strands 6 through 12 in full, plus the earlier sub-points this half of the course also reaches. Sub-points not listed (1.1-1.3, 2.1-2.2, 3.x, 4.1-4.3, 5.2-5.3) belong to the first half of the course and are indexed there. Standards codes never appear on student pages. Modules, not weeks, are the governing order.

The "Submitted" column lists graded work students do in the module: two Primary Source Exercises, the Discussion, and the module's Assignment. The Quarter 3 Exam (Module 27), Quarter 4 Exam (Module 36) and the Semester Final draw on all of the weekly banks; they are not listed per standard.

assignments.title: Module 20 VR Activity
assignments.html:
In this activity you will use your VR headset to study the ground at Vicksburg. Enter the immersive session your teacher has assigned for this module. [TBD: user: session or location name, and how the student reaches it]

Spend time in two places: at river level, and up on the bluffs. Move around. Look in every direction. Then answer the three prompts below in one submission. Write in complete sentences. About 150 to 250 words in all is enough.

If you do not have access to a headset, [TBD: user: confirm alternate path for students without a headset].

Prompts:

  1. Standing on the bluffs, what could a Confederate gunner see and control? Standing at river level, what would a Union boat pilot see? Describe the difference in two or three sentences.
  2. Use what you saw to explain why Grant crossed the river below Vicksburg instead of attacking the bluffs again. Use one fact from Lesson 20.1.
  3. Choose one detail from Mary Ann Loughborough's account of the siege. Explain how the ground at Vicksburg helped create that detail.

assignments.title: Module 21 Primary Source Report
assignments.html:
Write a short report on this module's two primary sources: the Confederate Exemption Act (Primary Source 21.1) and the soldier's letter or petition (Primary Source 21.2). About 300 to 400 words is enough. Use complete sentences and give your report these three parts.

  1. What each source says. In two or three sentences for each source, say what it asks for, orders, or claims, and who wrote it. Use a short phrase from the source in your own sentence if it helps.
  2. What the two sources show together. The war asked different things of different people. Explain how these two sources, side by side, show that. Use one fact from this module's lessons.
  3. What you cannot tell. Name one thing neither source can tell you about the war in Mississippi, and say why.

assignments.title: Module 23 VR Activity
assignments.html:
In this activity you will use your VR headset to stand inside a place that mattered in the story of Reconstruction. Enter the immersive session your teacher has assigned for this module. [TBD: user: session or location name, whether the space is a Senate chamber, a freedpeople's schoolhouse, or another place, and how the student reaches it]

Spend time in the space. Look at who and what is in it, and imagine who would have been there in 1870. Then answer the three prompts below in one submission. Write in complete sentences. About 150 to 250 words in all is enough.

If you do not have access to a headset, [TBD: user: confirm alternate path for students without a headset].

Prompts:

  1. Describe the space in two or three sentences. Who would have been in it in 1870, and who would not have been allowed in it a decade earlier?
  2. Choose Hiram Revels or a student in one of the first public schools. Using one fact from Lesson 23.2, explain what that person might have felt standing here.
  3. The Constitution of 1868 and the Senate both depended on the support of people who held power. Name one thing that could have gone wrong for the new order, and say why it mattered.

assignments.title: Module 24 Primary Source Report
assignments.html:
Write a short report on this module's two primary sources: the Boutwell Report testimony on the Clinton riot (Primary Source 24.1) and Senator Blanche K. Bruce's speech on the Mississippi election (Primary Source 24.2). About 300 to 400 words is enough. Use complete sentences and give your report these three parts.

  1. What each source says. In two or three sentences for each source, say who is speaking, what happened or what is being asked for, and who the speaker hoped would act. Use a short phrase from the source in your own sentence if it helps.
  2. What the two sources show together. One source describes violence around an election. The other asks the national government to respond. Explain what the two sources, side by side, show about how Reconstruction ended in Mississippi. Use one fact from this module's lessons.
  3. What you cannot tell. Name one thing neither source can tell you about the 1875 election, and say why.

assignments.title: Module 26 VR Activity
assignments.html:
In this activity you will use your VR headset to stand inside a place that shaped daily life for Black Mississippians in the years after 1890. Enter the immersive session your teacher has assigned for this module. [TBD: user: session or location name, whether the space is a train car, a Delta plantation, a church, a schoolhouse, or another place, and how the student reaches it]

Spend time in the space. Look at who and what is in it, and think about who could enter freely, who could not, and who decided. Then answer the three prompts below in one submission. Write in complete sentences. About 150 to 250 words in all is enough.

If you do not have access to a headset, [TBD: user: confirm alternate path for students without a headset].

Prompts:

  1. Describe the space in two or three sentences. Who would have used it around 1900, and who would have decided the rules for it?
  2. Using one fact from Lesson 26.1 or Lesson 26.2, explain how law or custom shaped what a Black Mississippian could do in this place.
  3. Ida B. Wells left Mississippi, and many others stayed. Pick one of those choices and say which pressure, such as danger, debt, family, land, or opportunity, mattered most to a person in this space.

assignments.title: Module 27 Primary Source Report
assignments.html:
Write a short report on this module's two primary sources: the Chicago Defender's reports on the 1927 flood camps (Primary Source 27.1) and the Flood Control Act of 1928 (Primary Source 27.2). About 300 to 400 words is enough. Use complete sentences and give your report these three parts.

questions.text: Before you read anything this week, write your first answer to this question in two or three sentences: Why did Mississippi leave the Union in 1861, and could it have gone another way? It is fine to be unsure. You will answer it again at the end of the module.
I have looked at the objectives at the top of Lesson 19.1 and Lesson 19.2.

Not yet. I will before I begin.

quizzes.title: Module 19 Reading Quiz
quizzes.description: Choose the best answer for each question. You may use your lesson notes.

questions.text: In the secession debate, support for waiting was strongest in the northeastern hills and the pine woods, where fewer families owned enslaved people. What does this pattern suggest?

answers.text: Everyone in the hill country wanted to stay in the Union no matter what happened.
The hill country had no cotton farms at all, so its delegates took no side in the debate.
Support for waiting was stronger where fewer people owned enslaved people.
The convention chose its delegates by lot, so they did not stand for any group of voters.

questions.feedback_correct: Lesson 19.1 notes that opinion differed by place, which is one reason the 84 to 15 vote can look more settled than it was.

questions.text: Abraham Lincoln promised not to end slavery where it already existed, yet many Mississippi leaders still feared his election. Which belief best explains the fear?

answers.text: They thought he would tax cotton so heavily that planters could no longer make a profit.
They thought he would draft Mississippians into the Union army as soon as he took office.
They thought he would lead the Northern states out of the Union to form a new country.
They believed slavery had to keep spreading, and he opposed its spread into the territories.

questions.feedback_correct: Many leaders believed that stopping slavery's growth would slowly squeeze it until it died.

questions.text: The Declaration of Causes says, "For far less cause than this, our fathers separated from the Crown of England." Why would the delegates compare themselves to the founders?

answers.text: To present secession as a justified act in the tradition of American independence.
To admit that the delegates knew they were breaking the law and meant to pay the price.
To ask Britain for help in the war that the delegates expected to come with the North.
To argue that the Constitution had been repealed by the Northern states.

questions.feedback_correct: The comparison is an argument. Whether it holds up is a fair question, since the founders did not defend an order in which most people had no rights.

questions.text: Some people say the Civil War was about "states' rights." The Declaration of Causes complains that Northern states used their own power to block a federal law that protected slavery. What does that complaint suggest?

answers.text: The document never mentions any state and speaks only of the nation as a whole in its text.
The document defended slavery, and it argued for states' rights only when that helped.
The document praised Northern state governments for protecting the liberty of their citizens.
The document argued that the federal government was too weak to collect taxes in the South.

questions.feedback_correct: The document is mainly about slavery, and it says so.

questions.text: The Anaconda Plan called for the Union to take control of the Mississippi River. Why would that help defeat the Confederacy?

answers.text: It would give the Union every Southern railroad running across the Confederate states.
It would end the blockade of Southern ports, which no longer served any purpose.
It would force Mississippi to rejoin the Union as soon as the river was opened.
It would split the Confederacy in two and cut Texas, Louisiana, and Arkansas off.

questions.feedback_correct: The river also carried cotton, soldiers, and supplies, so controlling it hurt the Confederacy in several ways.

questions.text: Confederate commander Albert Sidney Johnston was killed on the first day at Shiloh, and many historians think the battle might have gone differently had he lived. What does this show about how wars unfold?

answers.text: Armies never recover after they lose a commander in the middle of a large battle.
Commanders rarely matter to the outcome of a battle once the armies are in the field.
Outcomes can turn on what happens to one leader, so they are not fixed in advance.
Battles are decided only by the number of soldiers each side brings to the field.

questions.feedback_correct: Lesson 19.2 asks you to notice how choices and chance, not only numbers, shaped events.

questions.text: Confederate attacks at Iuka in September 1862 and at Corinth in October 1862 both failed. Why did those failures matter beyond the two towns?

answers.text: They left northern Mississippi in Union hands and weakened the river's defenders.
They ended the Union blockade of Southern ports and opened the coast to trade.
They convinced Mississippi to leave the Confederacy and ask for peace with the North.
They caused the Union to give up the Anaconda Plan and withdraw from the river valley.

questions.feedback_correct: By the end of 1862, Union armies held northern Mississippi, and only Vicksburg and Port Hudson still kept the Union from the whole river.

quizzes.title: Primary Source Exercise 19.1
quizzes.description: Read Primary Source 19.1, then answer the four questions. You may reopen the source while you answer. Choose the best answer for each question.

questions.text: A student claims that Mississippi left the Union mainly over tariffs. Which feature of the Declaration of Causes would best challenge that claim?

answers.text: Its long discussion of the tariff of 1828.
Its request for help from foreign governments.
Its silence about every issue except taxes.
Its central argument is about slavery and the danger the delegates saw to it.

questions.feedback_correct: The delegates wrote the declaration to explain their reasons, and the document centers on slavery.

questions.text: Suppose the secession convention had voted to leave the Union but had published no explanation. What would historians most likely have lost?

answers.text: A statement, in the delegates' own words, of why they acted.
The legal effect of the vote to secede.
Any record that a convention was held.
The names of the delegates who attended.

questions.feedback_correct: The ordinance carried the legal effect, and the journal records the meeting. Only the declaration gives the delegates' stated reasons.

questions.text: The convention voted 84 to 15 to secede. What does the fifteen-vote minority best show about secession in Mississippi?

answers.text: Mississippians had already agreed on secession for decades.
The convention had no real power to decide the question.
The delegates were chosen from only one party.
Leaving the Union was a contested choice, not a unanimous one.

questions.feedback_correct: A large majority voted to leave, but fifteen delegates voted no, so the outcome was not automatic.

questions.text: Why would the delegates write their reasons in a public declaration instead of only passing a law?

answers.text: Federal law required every state to publish its reasons.
They wanted to justify their decision to Mississippians, to other states, and to the wider world.
They were asking Congress for permission to secede.
They needed a document to set the date for new elections.

questions.feedback_correct: A declaration is an argument addressed to an audience. It is not a law.

quizzes.title: Primary Source Exercise 19.2
quizzes.description: Read Primary Source 19.2, then answer the four questions. You may reopen the source while you answer. Choose the best answer for each question.

questions.text: Why did Jefferson Davis speak in the Senate on January 21, 1861?

answers.text: He had just been elected president of the Confederacy.
He had been expelled from the Senate for treason.
Mississippi had voted to leave the Union, so he was giving up his Senate seat.
He wanted to propose a new compromise to Congress.

questions.feedback_correct: Davis spoke after Mississippi's secession. He became Confederate president only weeks later.

questions.text: Davis defends secession by describing the Union as an agreement the states had entered freely. Which idea is he applying?

answers.text: The belief that the Supreme Court decides all disputes among states.
The belief that states joined voluntarily and may withdraw.
The belief that the president holds all war powers.
The belief that citizens choose their national government directly.

questions.feedback_correct: This is the compact view of the Union, the main constitutional argument for secession.

questions.text: Suppose Davis had stayed in the Senate after Mississippi seceded. What problem would he most likely have faced?

answers.text: He would have been serving in a government that his own state no longer accepted.
He would have lost his right to vote in Mississippi.
He would have been forced to command the Union army.
He would have been named president of the Senate.

questions.feedback_correct: Davis's loyalty was to Mississippi's decision, and staying would have placed him against it.

questions.text: Which description best fits how Davis presents himself in this speech?

answers.text: As a man eager for war and angry at every senator.
As a man who has not yet decided what to do.
As a man doing a painful duty to his state, without personal hostility toward his colleagues.
As a man asking the Senate to punish Mississippi.

questions.feedback_correct: Davis speaks with regret and courtesy, which tells us how he wanted his action to be understood.

questions.text: Why did Grant move his army south of Vicksburg and cross the river at Bruinsburg?

answers.text: Direct attacks on Vicksburg from the north had failed, and south of the city he could reach firm ground east of the river.
Confederate troops had left Vicksburg entirely.
President Lincoln ordered him to avoid the city.
The river was too shallow to cross anywhere else.

questions.feedback_correct: The northern approaches were swamps and bluffs that favored the defenders. The southern crossing opened a new line of attack.

questions.text: Suppose the Union Navy had not been able to run its ships past the Vicksburg guns. What would most likely have been a problem for Grant?

answers.text: He would have had too many supplies.
He would have had no enemy to fight.
He would have lacked boats to carry his army across the river south of the city.
He would have been forced to surrender the army.

questions.feedback_correct: Grant's plan depended on naval vessels to ferry his troops.

questions.text: Grant moved away from his main supply base and lived partly off the land. Which trait of character does this decision best show?

answers.text: A habit of waiting for orders from Washington.
A fear of losing his army.
An unwillingness to leave the river.
A willingness to take a calculated risk and act decisively.

questions.feedback_correct: A commander who cuts loose from his supplies accepts danger for a chance at a larger gain.

questions.text: Grant wrote his memoirs in 1885, more than twenty years after the campaign. Why should a historian compare his account with reports written in 1863?

answers.text: Memoirs always contain the exact words of every order.
Reports from 1863 were never kept.
Grant had never been to Mississippi.
Memory and hindsight can change how a writer describes what he planned and felt.

questions.feedback_correct: A memoir is written looking back, so it may smooth or shape the story.

quizzes.title: Primary Source Exercise 20.2
quizzes.description: Read Primary Source 20.2, then answer the four questions. You may reopen the source while you answer. Choose the best answer for each question.

questions.text: Why did many families in Vicksburg dig caves during the siege?

answers.text: To hide supplies from Confederate soldiers.
To protect themselves from the shells that fell on the town.
To prepare an escape through Union lines.
To store cotton for sale.

questions.feedback_correct: Union gunboats and artillery shelled the town for weeks.

questions.text: Loughborough describes the siege from the view of one Confederate officer's wife. What is the most important limit of using her book as evidence?

answers.text: It was written by someone who was not present.
It cannot be used because it was printed.
It shows one family's view and leaves out the experience of many other people in Vicksburg.
It describes events from a different war.

questions.feedback_correct: A single account is real evidence, but it is one perspective. Enslaved and Black residents, for example, are not at the center.

questions.text: Suppose Vicksburg's defenders had been well supplied with food throughout the siege. How might the civilians' experience have been different?

answers.text: Hunger would have played a smaller part in the pressure on the town to surrender.
The shelling would have stopped.
The caves would have become unnecessary.
The Union army would have left.

questions.feedback_correct: Shortages of food were a major pressure during the siege.

questions.text: The book was published in 1864, while the war was still being fought. How might that have shaped what Loughborough wrote?

answers.text: Readers at the time were still part of the war, so she may have chosen what to stress with them in mind.
She had no readers.
She wrote after the Confederacy had surrendered.
She was forbidden to describe the siege.

questions.feedback_correct: A book written during a war is part of that war's public argument.

questions.text: Why did the Confederate Congress pass a law excusing some men from military service?

answers.text: It wanted to end the draft altogether.
It wanted to raise money from foreign banks.
It wanted to arm enslaved men.
It wanted to keep farms and plantations producing while the army grew.

questions.feedback_correct: The Exemption Act balanced the army's need for men against the need for food and cotton.

questions.text: Many poor white Southerners complained that this law favored the rich. Which idea best describes their complaint?

answers.text: That the army had too many officers.
That cotton should be taxed.
That the burdens of war were falling unevenly across classes.
That the Union had not declared war.

questions.feedback_correct: People felt it was a rich man's war and a poor man's fight.

questions.text: Suppose the law had excused no one. What would most likely have happened on large plantations?

answers.text: Enslaved people would have been freed at once.
Planters would have stopped growing crops.
More of the men who managed them would have been drafted, leaving fewer to oversee the work.
The Union army would have left Mississippi.

questions.text: What does the law show about the link between slavery and the Confederate war effort?

The government thought slavery was unimportant.
The government forbade overseers from working.
The government treated keeping control of enslaved labor as part of what the war effort needed.

That military service creates a claim on the government.

questions.text: Why are a soldier's own letters valuable to historians compared with an officer's report?

They were written long after the war ended.
They were written by government lawyers.

questions.feedback_correct: Letters show what soldiers thought and wanted, but like any source they have a point of view.

questions.text: Suppose Black men had not been allowed to enlist in the Union army. What would most likely have been different for freedpeople?

They would have been sent back to slavery.
They would have no interest in the war.
They would have had a weaker claim to be treated as citizens after the war.

questions.feedback_correct: Military service became an important basis for arguments about citizenship.

High officials always grant requests.
Local planters could not read.
Petitions may be sent only to presidents.

He aimed at the Confederacy's means of making war, not only at its soldiers.
He wanted to force Mississippi's civilians into the Union army to fill its ranks.
He wanted to protect the railroads so that the Union could use them for its own supplies.

questions.feedback_correct: Wrecking railroads and storehouses was a way of ending an enemy's ability to supply its armies.

questions.text: The Confederates repaired part of the railroad damage at Meridian within weeks. What does this suggest about the expedition?

answers.text: It destroyed the Confederate army completely in a single campaign through the state.
It freed all of the enslaved people in the state within a few weeks of the march.
It ended the war in Mississippi and brought lasting peace to the whole region.
It hurt the Confederacy's rail network but did not end its ability to fight.

questions.feedback_correct: The expedition did real damage, but its effects did not last long, and the Union cavalry column that was supposed to join Sherman never arrived.

questions.text: Nathan Bedford Forrest beat a larger Union force at Brice's Crossroads in June 1864, and Union commanders kept trying to catch him. What lesson did Union leaders draw?

answers.text: Holding Mississippi's towns and railroads did not mean controlling the countryside.
Cavalry could not fight well in the kind of country that is found in the state of Mississippi.
Forrest would never be seen again by Union soldiers after such a hard fight in June.
The Union should give up its efforts in the state after the loss of so many men.

questions.feedback_correct: Lesson 22.1 uses Forrest to show that the war in Mississippi was not over when the Union held the river.

questions.text: At the end of the war, Mississippi faced two problems at once: keeping order and producing enough for people to live well. Which fact best shows the second problem?

answers.text: Governor Clark was arrested by Union troops and held in a prison in the North.
General Taylor surrendered in Alabama and ended the fighting east of the river.
Railroads were torn up, many farms had lost livestock and fences, and many banks failed.
President Johnson appointed a provisional governor to lead the state in the summer.

questions.feedback_correct: A wrecked economy made it hard for people to produce enough to live on.

questions.text: The Black Code let freedpeople marry legally and sue in court. It also required a written labor contract each January. What does this combination suggest about the lawmakers' aim?

answers.text: They wanted to treat Black and white Mississippians the same way under the law.
They were willing to recognize some rights but wanted to keep Black workers tied to white landowners.
They wanted to bring Northern workers to Mississippi to replace the freedpeople on the farms.
They were trying to end the Freedmen's Bureau by making its work seem unneeded.

questions.feedback_correct: Some rights were granted, while the contract and vagrancy rules limited Black workers' freedom to leave a job.

questions.text: In December 1865, Mississippi's legislature voted not to ratify the Thirteenth Amendment. What does this suggest about how many white leaders saw emancipation?

answers.text: They had always supported it and hoped to see it become the law of the whole country.
They believed it was only a state matter and had no place in the national Constitution.
They had never heard of it and so did not understand what the vote was about.
Many accepted it only reluctantly, as something forced on them by the war.

questions.feedback_correct: The 1865 convention also wrote slavery out of the state constitution only reluctantly.

questions.text: Freedmen's Bureau agents found that local courts often refused to punish the people who attacked freedpeople. What does this show?

answers.text: A law that promises protection means little when the men enforcing it are unwilling.
The courts had no power at all to hear any case brought by a freedperson.
Freedpeople never asked the courts for help with any problem that they faced.
The Bureau had given up on Mississippi and withdrawn all of its agents from the state.

questions.feedback_correct: The Black Codes were enforced by white county officials, which shaped how they worked in practice.

questions.text: Freed families disliked working in gangs under an overseer and preferred sharecropping, even though it had serious flaws. What does this choice suggest?

answers.text: Freed families had no opinion about how they worked and took whatever terms were offered.
Freed families used what little power they had to gain control over their own time and family life.

questions.text: A sharecropping family bought supplies on credit from a merchant who held a lien on the crop. Why did this arrangement so often leave families in debt?

answers.text: Merchants refused to give credit to farm families and demanded cash for every purchase.
The price of cotton rose every year, so families kept borrowing against a bigger crop.
Families were paid in advance for the whole crop and then spent the money too soon.
Credit prices and interest were higher than cash prices, and a poor crop left families still owing.

questions.feedback_correct: A family that could not pay off its debt started the next year behind, and the cycle repeated.

Families paid off their debts quickly and began to buy land in the Delta.
Merchants stopped selling on credit, and so the families had to grow their own food.

questions.feedback_correct: Falling prices pushed families to grow more cotton, and more cotton pushed prices down further.

The clause required every voter to pass a written test that was graded by judges of the Supreme Court.
The clause applied only to officials who wanted to register new voters in their counties.
The clause banned registrars from using their own judgment and gave them a fixed list of answers.

questions.feedback_correct: A white farmer who could not read well might be told he understood, and a Black teacher might be told he did not.

questions.feedback_correct: Lesson 25.2 says both sides can agree that he had no good choices, even though they disagree about what he should have done.

It did what its writers wanted by shrinking the Black electorate without naming race.
It was overturned by the federal courts within a year of being put into effect.
It showed that Black men chose not to register in large numbers of their own free will.

questions.feedback_correct: The rules were written in neutral language, but their effect was to disfranchise most Black voters.

questions.text: Why did Ida B. Wells leave Memphis?

answers.text: She had been offered a post in Congress.
She had been hired by a Northern school.
She had been elected mayor.
A mob destroyed her newspaper office and threatened her life after she wrote about lynchings.

questions.feedback_correct: Her reporting made her a target.

questions.text: People who defended lynching often said it punished serious crimes. How did Wells answer that claim?

answers.text: She agreed with the claim.
She ignored the cases.
She gathered facts about the cases and showed that the usual explanation did not match the evidence.
She said the cases were fiction.

questions.feedback_correct: Her method was to investigate and report.

questions.text: Suppose Wells had published her findings only in Memphis. What would most likely have happened?

answers.text: Lynching would have ended at once.
Every reader in the country would have heard.
Local pressure could have silenced her, and fewer readers outside the South would have learned what she found.
The newspaper would have grown.

questions.feedback_correct: Publishing in the North gave her reach beyond the mob's control.

questions.text: A mob that kills a man instead of letting a court decide shows the failure of which basic task of government?

answers.text: Collecting taxes.
Building schools.
Printing money.
Keeping order and applying the law fairly to all.

questions.feedback_correct: A government that lets mobs replace courts has failed at its core duty.

quizzes.description: Read Primary Source 26.2, then answer the four questions. You may reopen the source while you answer. Choose the best answer for each question.

questions.text: The law required "equal" accommodations in separate cars. What question should a careful reader ask about that word?

answers.text: Which railroad is oldest?
What in the law ensures the cars will in fact be equal?
How many cars should a train have?
Who invented railroads?

questions.feedback_correct: The promise of equality is only as strong as the means of enforcing it.

questions.text: How did the separate-car law fit into the larger pattern of the 1880s and 1890s?

answers.text: It reversed Reconstruction's rules.
It was the first law to abolish slavery.
It had no connection to other laws.
It was an early step in a growing system of segregation in public places.

questions.feedback_correct: Segregation spread from trains to many parts of daily life.

questions.text: Suppose the law had included no penalty for railroads that broke it. What would most likely have been true?

answers.text: Trains would have stopped running.
Enforcement would have been weak, and railroads might have ignored it.
Every railroad would have obeyed.
The law would have applied to buses.

questions.feedback_correct: Without penalties, rules depend on goodwill.

questions.text: Who bore the main burden of enforcement and its penalties?

answers.text: Only the governor.
Only the legislature.
Railroad workers and passengers, with Black passengers most affected.
Only the Supreme Court.

questions.feedback_correct: Laws like this shaped everyday travel for Black Mississippians.

quizzes.title: Primary Source Exercise 27.1
quizzes.description: Read Primary Source 27.1, then answer the four questions. You may reopen the source while you answer. Choose the best answer for each question.

questions.text: Why did the Chicago Defender send reporters to cover conditions in the 1927 flood camps?

answers.text: It was owned by the Mississippi governor.
It wanted to sell farmland.
It was ordered to by Congress.
Its readers across the country, including many who had left the South, wanted to know what was happening to Black Mississippians.

questions.feedback_correct: The Defender was a Black-owned paper with a national audience.

questions.text: Mississippi's own newspapers described the camps differently. What should a historian do with two such accounts?

answers.text: Pick whichever account is shorter.
Assume both are equally accurate.
Compare them and ask who wrote each, for whom, and why.
Throw out both.

questions.feedback_correct: Different authors have different interests.

questions.text: Suppose the Defender had not reported on the camps. What would most likely have been true?

answers.text: The camps would have closed.
The flood would not have happened.
Fewer people outside the Delta would have learned about conditions and restrictions in them.
Every Mississippi newspaper would have reported the same story.

questions.feedback_correct: The Defender carried information that local papers did not.

questions.text: How might such reports have affected the Great Migration?

answers.text: They could strengthen readers' decisions to leave for northern cities.
They stopped migration entirely.
They convinced people to move to the Delta.
They had no effect at all.

questions.feedback_correct: News about treatment in the South helped shape the choice to leave.

quizzes.title: Primary Source Exercise 27.2
quizzes.description: Read Primary Source 27.2, then answer the four questions. You may reopen the source while you answer. Choose the best answer for each question.

questions.text: Why did Congress pass the Flood Control Act of 1928?

answers.text: Congress wanted to end the Army Corps of Engineers.
The river had dried up.
The 1927 flood showed that local levee boards could not control the Mississippi alone.
The states had asked Congress to close the river.

questions.feedback_correct: The flood exposed the limits of the old system.

questions.text: The act made the national government responsible for a problem too large for local governments. Which idea does that show?

answers.text: That national government can take on tasks that states and localities cannot manage alone.
That states must handle everything.
That rivers cannot be governed.
That only cities can build levees.

questions.feedback_correct: It is an example of federal power expanding to meet a large need.

questions.text: Suppose Congress had not passed the act. What would most likely have remained true?

answers.text: The Army Corps would have built every levee.
The river would have stopped flooding.
Levee building would have stayed mostly with local and state boards that had just been overwhelmed.
All levees would have been removed.

questions.feedback_correct: The law shifted responsibility upward.

questions.text: How did the law change the relationship between Mississippi and Washington?

answers.text: It made Mississippi independent.
It ended federal involvement.
It moved the capital.
It increased the role of the federal government in the state's daily affairs.

questions.feedback_correct: A federal project meant federal money, rules, and engineers in the state.

quizzes.title: Quarter 3 Exam
quizzes.description: Choose the best answer for each question. Each question stands on its own.

questions.text: At Mississippi's secession convention the vote to leave was 84 to 15. Why does that number not show the whole picture of opinion in the state?

answers.text: The delegates were chosen by lot rather than by vote, so they did not truly represent any group of voters.
Every delegate from the hill country voted to leave, which hid how much disagreement existed in the east.
Support for waiting was stronger where fewer families owned enslaved people, so opinion differed by region.
Mississippi had no cotton farms in 1861, so the vote was only a symbolic one that meant very little.

questions.feedback_correct: Opinion differed by place, which is one reason the vote can look more settled than it was.

questions.text: Abraham Lincoln promised not to end slavery where it already existed, yet many Mississippi leaders feared his election. Which belief best explains the fear?

answers.text: They believed slavery had to keep spreading to survive, and he opposed its spread into the territories.
They thought he would tax cotton so heavily that no planter in the state could hope to make a profit.
They thought he would draft young Mississippians into the Union army during his first year in office.
They thought he would lead the Northern states out of the Union and form a new country of their own.

questions.feedback_correct: Many leaders believed that stopping slavery's growth would slowly squeeze it until it died.

questions.text: The Anaconda Plan called for the Union to take control of the Mississippi River. Why would that help defeat the Confederacy?

answers.text: It would give the Union control of every Southern railroad that ran from east to west across the South.
It would end the Union blockade of Southern ports, because the blockade would no longer be needed.
It would force Mississippi to rejoin the Union as soon as the river was opened to Union ships.
It would split the Confederacy in two, cutting Texas, Louisiana, and Arkansas off from the rest.

questions.feedback_correct: The river also carried cotton, soldiers, and supplies, so controlling it hurt the Confederacy in several ways.

questions.text: Why did Grant move his army south of Vicksburg and cross the river at Bruinsburg?

answers.text: The Confederate troops had left Vicksburg, so no one remained in the city who could stop a crossing.
Attacks from the north had failed, and below the city he could reach firm ground east of the river.
President Lincoln had ordered him to avoid the city and march on toward the capital at Jackson.
The river was too wide to cross anywhere north of the city during that season of high water.

questions.feedback_correct: Attacks from the north had failed, so Grant looked for a way onto high ground east of the river.

questions.text: Suppose the Union Navy had not been able to run its ships past the Vicksburg guns. What would most likely have been Grant's problem?

answers.text: He would have had so many supplies that his army could not move quickly.
He would have had no enemy to fight on the east side of the river.
He would have been forced to surrender his army to the Confederates at once.
He would have lacked boats to carry his army across the river south of the city.

questions.feedback_correct: The navy's ships were needed to carry the army across the river below Vicksburg.

questions.text: Why did many families in Vicksburg dig caves during the siege?

answers.text: To protect themselves from the shells that fell on the town.
To hide food and supplies from Confederate soldiers who wanted to take them.
To prepare a secret path of escape through the Union lines around the city.
To store cotton safely until it could be sold after the war ended.

questions.feedback_correct: Shells fell on the town day after day, and caves offered shelter.

questions.text: Many poor white Southerners complained that the Confederate law excusing some men from military service favored the rich. What was their complaint?

answers.text: The army had too many officers and not enough common soldiers.
Cotton should have been taxed more heavily to pay for the war effort.
The burdens of the war were falling unevenly across the classes.
The Union had never formally declared war on the Confederate states.

questions.feedback_correct: A slogan spread across the South: a rich man's war and a poor man's fight.

questions.text: Why did the Confederate Congress pass a law excusing some men from military service?

answers.text: It wanted to end the draft altogether and rely on volunteers from every county.
It wanted to keep order and production going on large plantations while the army grew.
It wanted to raise money from foreign banks by excusing wealthy men from service.
It wanted to arm enslaved men so that fewer white men would be needed.

questions.feedback_correct: Leaders argued that someone had to keep order on large plantations and keep the crops growing.

questions.text: Why are a Union soldier's own letters valuable to historians compared with an officer's report?

answers.text: They give his own view of events, which officers' reports often leave out.
They are always more accurate than any other kind of source from the war.
They were written long after the war ended, when memories were clearest.
They were written by government lawyers who checked every statement.

questions.feedback_correct: Letters show what soldiers thought and wanted, but like any source they have a point of view.

questions.text: In his report, Sherman said that the town of Meridian was "gone." He meant that its depots, storehouses, and military buildings no longer existed. What does this show about his aim?

answers.text: He wanted to capture the Confederate capital and end the war at once.
He wanted to force Mississippi's civilians to join the Union army.
He wanted to protect the railroads so that Union forces could use them later.
He aimed at the Confederacy's means of making war, not only at its soldiers.

questions.feedback_correct: Wrecking railroads and storehouses was a way of ending an enemy's ability to supply its armies.

questions.text: The Black Code let freedpeople marry legally and sue in court. It also required a written labor contract each January. What does this combination suggest about the lawmakers' aim?

answers.text: They wanted to treat Black and white Mississippians the same way under the law, in the courts and at work.
They were willing to recognize some rights but wanted to keep Black workers tied to white landowners.
They wanted to bring Northern workers into Mississippi to take the place of the freedpeople.
They were trying to end the Freedmen's Bureau by making its work seem unnecessary to Congress.

questions.feedback_correct: Some rights were granted, while the contract and vagrancy rules limited Black workers' freedom to leave a job.

questions.text: Freedmen's Bureau agents found that local courts often refused to punish the people who attacked freedpeople. What does this show?

answers.text: The courts had no power to hear any case brought by a freedperson, whatever the facts of the case.
Freedpeople never asked the courts for help with any problem, so the Bureau's agents had nothing to see.
A law that promises protection means little when the men enforcing it are unwilling.
The Freedmen's Bureau had given up on Mississippi and withdrawn all of its agents from the state.

questions.feedback_correct: The Black Codes were enforced by white county officials, which shaped how they worked in practice.

questions.text: Hiram Revels was chosen for a Senate seat once held by Jefferson Davis. Why is that fact meaningful?

answers.text: It proves that Revels was related to Jefferson Davis through marriage.
It shows how much Mississippi's politics had changed in about a decade.
It shows that Davis had never really left the Senate at all.
It means the seat had been abolished and then created again for Revels.

questions.feedback_correct: A Black senator in the seat Davis left in 1861 marked a sharp change.

questions.text: Why did Black Mississippians help write the Constitution of 1868?

answers.text: The Confederate government ordered a new constitution to be written before the war was over.
Black delegates were appointed to the convention by the governor without any vote being held.
The Supreme Court demanded that the state write a new constitution in a ruling about Mississippi's laws.
The Reconstruction Acts gave Black men the vote and called a convention elected by the new voters.

questions.feedback_correct: Congress required a new constitution under the Reconstruction Acts, and Black men could now vote for the delegates.

questions.text: The 1868 constitution set up public schools open to all children. Which idea about government does that reflect?

answers.text: That a republic needs educated citizens, and the government has a role in providing for it.
That education is a private matter that each family must handle alone, at its own cost.
That schools should be run entirely by churches and charities, with no role for the state.
That education is useful only for children from wealthy families who can afford to attend.

questions.feedback_correct: Public schooling treats education as part of the common good.

questions.text: What was the main purpose of Ku Klux Klan violence in Mississippi in the early 1870s?

answers.text: To enforce federal law in counties where there were too few marshals to do so.
To protect public schools from being closed for lack of money in the state treasury.
To use fear to keep Black voters and Republican leaders out of politics.
To collect taxes for the state in counties that had refused to pay what was owed.

questions.feedback_correct: The Klan's purpose was political. A man who is afraid to go to the polls does not vote.

questions.text: Why did the Democratic campaign of 1875, often called the Mississippi Plan, succeed?

answers.text: Many Republicans switched parties after the Democrats offered them jobs in the new government.
Congress abolished the Republican Party in Mississippi shortly before the election was held.
The Supreme Court ordered a new election to be held, and the Democrats won that vote easily.
Armed Democratic clubs frightened Republican voters away from the polls, and Washington sent no help.

questions.feedback_correct: Violence and threats kept many Republican voters at home, and Governor Ames's request for troops was turned down.

questions.text: Some historians say Reconstruction in Mississippi was abandoned rather than overthrown. What does the word "abandoned" emphasize?

answers.text: A federal government that had the power to protect voters chose not to use it.
Black voters chose to leave politics once the first outbreak of violence had begun.
Republicans lost only because taxes had risen too high for the property owners.
Democrats had no part at all in the ending of Reconstruction in the state.

questions.feedback_correct: The two words point to two different parts of the story, and the truth probably needs both.

questions.text: Why did the crop lien system so often leave farm families in debt?

answers.text: Merchants paid cash for the crop in advance, so families spent it all before the harvest.
The price of cotton rose every year, so families kept on borrowing more and more.
Credit prices and interest were higher than cash prices, and a poor crop left the family still owing.
Families were forbidden to buy anything on credit and so were forced to go without it.

questions.feedback_correct: A family that could not pay off its debt started the next year behind.

questions.text: By the mid-1890s falling cotton prices pushed many families to plant even more cotton. Why was this a trap?

answers.text: Cotton became so scarce that families could not afford to buy seed.
More cotton pushed the price down further, so debts became harder to pay.
Merchants stopped buying cotton altogether once prices began to fall.
Cotton could no longer be sold anywhere, so the crop was left to rot.

questions.feedback_correct: Falling prices pushed families to grow more cotton, and more cotton pushed prices down further.

questions.text: The voting rules in Article 12 of Mississippi's Constitution of 1890 never mention race. Why did the writers use neutral wording?

answers.text: The Fifteenth Amendment forbids denying the vote because of race.
Mississippi had no Black voters at the time, so race did not need mention.
The Supreme Court had ordered the delegates to avoid the subject.
The delegates believed race was unimportant to the work of the convention.

questions.feedback_correct: The rules were written in neutral words, but their purpose was understood.

questions.text: What did the Supreme Court decide in Williams v. Mississippi in 1898, and what was an effect of the decision?

answers.text: It struck down the voting rules and ended the poll tax in Mississippi, which led other states to drop theirs.
It ordered Mississippi to seat Black jurors in every county in the state, which led to many changes.
It sent the case back to the state without any ruling on the rules, so nothing was changed in the law.
It let the rules stand because they did not mention race, which made it easier for other states to copy them.

questions.feedback_correct: The ruling gave legal cover to the Mississippi system, and other states followed it.

questions.text: Why did Ida B. Wells leave Memphis in 1892?

answers.text: She had been offered a seat in Congress and had to move to Washington to take it up.
A mob destroyed her newspaper office and warned her not to return after she reported on lynchings.
She had been elected mayor of a Northern town and took office there at the start of the year.
A Northern school had hired her as a teacher and paid for her trip north on the railroad.

questions.feedback_correct: Her reporting made her a target, and she carried her work to the North and to Britain.

questions.text: Mississippi's 1888 railroad law required "equal" separate cars for white and Black passengers. In practice, what often happened?

answers.text: The cars were identical in every way, and no one ever complained about them to the railroads.
Black passengers refused to ride the trains until the law was changed by the legislature.
The cars for Black passengers were often crowded and dirty, though the fare was the same.
The railroads ended segregation on their own within a few years of the law being passed.

questions.feedback_correct: The promise of equality was weak where nothing made sure the cars were equal.

questions.text: How did Parchman Farm, opened in 1901, relate to the older system of convict leasing?

answers.text: It ended the use of convict labor entirely and sent all of the state's prisoners home again.
It freed most of the state's convicts and closed the old jails that had held them for years.
It leased convicts only to railroads and not to planters or to the lumber camps of the state.
It was a state-run prison plantation, and many historians say it kept the same logic of cheap labor.

questions.feedback_correct: Parchman was a different system from leasing, but it still depended on the labor of prisoners.

questions.text: Which of these was a "push" factor that drove Black Mississippians to leave the state during the Great Migration?

answers.text: Jobs in Northern factories that paid higher wages than the farms.
Lynching and crushing debt.
The Illinois Central Railroad line that ran straight to Chicago.
Letters from relatives in the North describing work and better schools.

questions.feedback_correct: The other choices are "pull" factors that drew people toward the North.

questions.text: How did the Flood Control Act of 1928 change flood policy on the lower Mississippi River?

answers.text: The federal government took responsibility and agreed to pay most of the cost.
Each state took full control of its own levees and paid for them alone.
The act ended all levee building and left the river to find its own course.
The Red Cross took over flood control on the lower river from then on.

questions.feedback_correct: For the first time the national government treated a flood that crossed many states as a national problem.

questions.text: In 1927, why did many planters want Black refugees kept in the Delta relief camps?

answers.text: They wanted to save money on the cost of feeding the refugees.
The Red Cross required refugees to stay in the camps for a year.
They feared that workers who left the Delta would not come back.
No trains or roads led out of the Delta during the flood.

questions.feedback_correct: The reason was largely economic, and after the flood many Black families did leave.

questions.text: What was the main effect of mechanical cotton pickers, first put to work near Clarksdale in 1944?

answers.text: They raised cotton prices so much that new tenant families moved to the Delta.
They ended cotton farming in Mississippi within a few years of their arrival.
They brought so many new jobs that families moved into the Delta in large numbers.
Planters needed fewer workers, so sharecroppers were no longer needed.

questions.feedback_correct: Mechanization spread through the Delta over the next twenty years.

questions.text: What did Mississippi's Balance Agriculture With Industry program, begun in 1936, allow towns to do?

answers.text: Issue bonds to build factories and attract companies to their towns.
Pay farmers to grow less cotton so that the price of the crop would rise.
Draft workers into new factories that were built beside the cotton fields.
Sell Delta land to Northern investors who promised to build railroads.

questions.feedback_correct: The wages were low, but they were wages, and for Black families factory work was often closed or limited to the lowest-paid jobs.

quizzes.title: Module 28 Reading Quiz
quizzes.description: Choose the best answer for each question. You may use your lesson notes.

questions.text: Brown v. Board of Education said that separating children by race creates a sense of inferiority. Why did the Court begin with schools?

answers.text: Schools were the only segregated institution in the South at the time of the ruling.
Schools were the cheapest places to begin the work of change in the Southern states.
Southern schools had already begun to integrate by the time the Court heard the cases.
Schools shape what children become, so a child shut out of them loses later chances.

questions.feedback_correct: Lesson 28.1 says the Court started with schools because schools shape what children become.

questions.text: Just before Brown, Mississippi had begun to improve Black schools, hoping to prove that separate could be equal. What did the ruling show about that effort?

answers.text: It was too little and came too late to meet the Court's standard of equal schools.
It had already succeeded in making the Black schools equal to the white schools.
It was against the state law that had been passed in the years before the ruling.
It was copied by the Supreme Court and made the model for its own opinion.

questions.feedback_correct: Brown showed that the effort to make separate schools equal came too late.

questions.text: Members of the Citizens' Council were often bankers, merchants, and lawyers. Why did that make their pressure so effective?

answers.text: They commanded state troops and could send them to any home or workplace.
They sat on the federal courts and could decide the cases that were brought.
They controlled jobs, loans, and credit, so they could ruin a person without violence.
They wrote the rulings of the Supreme Court and so knew in advance what it would decide.

questions.feedback_correct: The Council's main weapon was money, and no one was whipped or shot to teach the lesson.

questions.text: Fifty-three Black parents in Yazoo City signed a school petition in 1955, and most later took their names off it. What does this show about the Council's methods?

answers.text: Parents no longer wanted desegregation once they had read the petition more closely.
Pressure on jobs and credit taught families that asking for their rights could ruin their lives.
The school board had agreed to integrate and so the petition was no longer needed.
A court had ordered the names removed because the petition had been signed in error.

questions.feedback_correct: Lesson 28.1 says the Council did not need violence to make its point.

questions.text: Lesson 28.1 calls Mississippi's answer to Brown "a choice, not a fate." Which fact best supports that claim?

answers.text: Mississippi's economy depended on cotton and cheap labor, which left leaders no room to change.
Leaders had other options, such as obeying and adjusting, and they turned those options down.
The Supreme Court had no power over the states and so could not have required a change.
The first Citizens' Council met in Indianola and set the course for the whole state.

questions.feedback_correct: The lesson says leaders were not forced into defiance by history.

questions.text: George Lee and Lamar Smith were both killed in 1955 for working to register voters. Why were registered voters treated as a threat?

answers.text: They were running for governor and so were seen as a danger to the sitting officials.
They had refused to pay their taxes and were being punished by the county.
They were members of the Citizens' Council who had broken with its leaders.
Where Black residents were a majority, a few registered voters could change who held office.

questions.feedback_correct: A vote was power, and some white leaders treated each new registration as a threat.

questions.text: In the Till case a trial was held and the jury acquitted both men. How does that differ from the Lee and Smith cases, and what does it show about the courts?

answers.text: A court can hold a trial and still fail to protect every person equally under the law.
Mississippi courts never held any trials in these years, whatever the crime.
The jury was mostly Black, and so it could not agree on a verdict in the case.
Double jeopardy allowed a second trial once the first jury had made its decision.

questions.feedback_correct: The lesson says the verdict said a Black child's life counted for less than a white man's word.

Schools should be run only by the federal government.
Segregation was not common in the South.
Separating children by race harms them and makes the schools unequal in fact.

answers.text: The dual school system could have continued legally, with the state working only to equalize facilities.

Every school would have integrated at once.
The Citizens' Councils would never have formed.

To call for a new constitution.

questions.text: Stokely Carmichael's call for Black Power alarmed some leaders. According to its supporters, what did it mean?

answers.text: That Black Americans should leave the country and start new lives somewhere else.
That Black Americans should give up voting and turn to other kinds of action.
That Black communities should gain political strength and take pride in their history.
That violence was the only path left after so many years of broken promises.

questions.feedback_correct: Critics feared it would divide the movement, but its supporters described it as political strength and pride.

questions.text: Black Mississippians ran one of the first Head Start programs in the nation, and some state leaders attacked it. What did the fight show?

answers.text: That Head Start was against the law and had to be closed down by order of the state.
It showed how much a Black-run program mattered, and how much some leaders resisted it.
That the program had no teachers and no children enrolled in it during its first year.
That schools in the state had already been fully integrated by the end of that year.

questions.feedback_correct: The fight over the Child Development Group of Mississippi showed both things.

questions.text: After the Voting Rights Act passed, Vernon Dahmer helped neighbors pay the poll tax and register at his store. Why was his home attacked?

answers.text: He was running for governor and so was seen as a danger to the sitting officials.
He had left the NAACP and so had lost the protection of its many members in the city.
He owned the town newspaper and had printed articles against the Klan.
The Klan used violence to stop efforts to put more Black citizens on the rolls.

questions.feedback_correct: Danger did not end with new laws.

questions.text: Many districts adopted freedom-of-choice plans after 1964, yet their schools stayed almost entirely separate. Why?

answers.text: Black families who chose a white school faced threats, lost jobs, and sometimes gunfire.
State law still required separate schools for every child in the state.
Black families did not want better schools and so chose to stay where they were.
No white schools were open to any student who wished to enroll in them.

questions.feedback_correct: In theory any family could pick any school, but in practice the cost of choosing fell on Black families.

questions.text: When schools were ordered to merge in 1969 and 1970, thousands of white families left the public schools. What was one result?

answers.text: Every district received equal funding and the same number of teachers.
Private academies closed within a year for lack of students and money.
All students were assigned to schools by a lottery run by the federal courts.
Many public schools became majority Black and often had less money than before.

questions.feedback_correct: The state was formally integrated, but many children still went to school with classmates of the same race.

questions.text: Lesson 31.2 says that school integration also cost Black communities something. What was it?

answers.text: Black students were barred from public colleges across the whole state.
Many Black schools were closed or merged, and Black teachers and principals lost jobs.
Black voters lost the vote that they had only just won in the years before.
Private academies took all of the public money that had been set aside for schools.

questions.feedback_correct: Change that opens one door can close another.

questions.text: The Sovereignty Commission lost its funding in 1973, and its files were later opened for anyone to read. What does this show?

answers.text: The Commission still operates in secret and keeps its files hidden from the public.
The files were all destroyed before anyone could read what they had said.
A government that once spied on citizens made its record public, so the truth could come out.
No one had ever been watched, and the files were only a set of old newspaper clippings.

questions.feedback_correct: A community that lets its records be read has begun to tell the truth about itself.
