quizzes.title: Quarter 4 Exam
quizzes.description: Choose the best answer for each question. Each question stands on its own.

questions.text: What did the Supreme Court decide in Brown v. Board of Education in 1954?

answers.text: Separate public schools for children of different races were unlawful because separation creates a sense of inferiority.
States could keep separate schools for each race as long as the schools were equal in quality and funding.
The Court left the question of school segregation to each state to decide for itself under its own laws.
Only segregation in colleges and universities was ended, while public schools were left as they were.

questions.feedback_correct: Chief Justice Earl Warren read a unanimous opinion.

questions.text: How did the Citizens' Council try to stop families from signing school desegregation petitions?

answers.text: It had the signers arrested by federal marshals and held in county jails for trial.
It closed every public school in the county by force of arms until the petitions ended.
It printed the signers' names and pressed on their jobs, loans, and credit.
It offered the signers jobs in other states if they would agree to leave Mississippi.

questions.feedback_correct: Pressure like this left no marks, but it taught families that asking for their rights could ruin their lives.

questions.text: What was the idea behind Mississippi's 1956 resolution of interposition?

answers.text: A state can stand between its people and the federal government and call a federal action unconstitutional.
Every federal court ruling must be approved by the state legislature before it can take effect in the state.
The president may overrule the Supreme Court whenever a state government objects to one of its rulings.
A county may secede from its state if it disagrees with a law passed by the legislature in Jackson.

questions.feedback_correct: The Supreme Court rejected this claim in 1958 in Cooper v. Aaron.

questions.text: Why did the death of Emmett Till reach so many people across the country?

answers.text: The trial ended in a conviction that the national newspapers reported in great detail for many weeks.
The killing took place in Chicago, where the national press was already watching events very closely.
Federal agents solved the case within days and then announced the result to the whole country.
His mother chose an open casket, and magazines and the Black press carried the photograph and story.

questions.feedback_correct: His mother refused to let the facts be hidden, and the growing reach of magazines and the Black press carried them far.

questions.text: What argument did Governor Ross Barnett give for refusing to admit James Meredith to Ole Miss?

answers.text: Meredith had not completed enough college credits to be admitted to the university.
The Supreme Court had no members from Mississippi and so could not rule on the case.
The Tenth Amendment leaves schools to the states, so the state had the last word.
The University of Mississippi was a private school that could choose its own students.

questions.feedback_correct: Barnett held this view sincerely, though the Supreme Court had rejected the claim in 1958.

questions.text: As the NAACP's first field secretary in Mississippi, what did Medgar Evers mainly do?

answers.text: He drove the back roads starting local chapters, urging people to register, and recording ignored killings.
He served as a federal marshal on the campus of Ole Miss during the crisis that took place in 1962.
He led the Citizens' Council chapter in Jackson and spoke for its members on local television shows.
He wrote the text of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and carried it to Congress for a final vote.

questions.feedback_correct: He also kept careful records so that the facts could not easily be denied.

questions.text: What did the opening of the Sovereignty Commission's files in 1998 make possible?

answers.text: The Commission could resume its work under a new name and with a new governor.
The people the Commission had watched could finally read what had been written about them.
The state could prove that no private citizen had ever been watched by its agents.
The files could be sold to private companies for use as evidence in civil lawsuits.

questions.feedback_correct: The files were sealed for years and opened only after a lawsuit.

questions.text: By 1964 only about seven in a hundred Black adults in Mississippi were registered to vote. Which pair of barriers best explains why?

answers.text: A literacy test judged by white registrars, and threats to jobs, loans, and homes.
A law that openly banned Black voting, and a rule that banned Black churches from meeting.
Too few polling places in the Delta, and a ban on Black newspapers in every county.
A rule that voters must own land, and a rule that voters must serve in the militia.

questions.feedback_correct: Each barrier made the next one easier to defend, and together they kept the rolls nearly all white.

questions.text: What was the purpose of the Freedom Vote of 1963?

answers.text: To elect a real governor who would take office in place of the sitting governor of the state.
To test a new kind of voting machine in the counties of the Mississippi Delta before an election.
To replace the state legislature with a council of ministers who were chosen by the Black churches.
To answer the claim that Black Mississippians did not want to vote, by holding a mock election.

questions.feedback_correct: About eighty thousand people voted. It did not change the law, but it changed the argument.

questions.text: At Atlantic City in 1964, what did party leaders offer the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party, and how did most delegates respond?

answers.text: Two at-large seats, which most delegates refused because they had come to be seated as the real delegation.
Full seating for every delegate they had chosen, which the delegation accepted with thanks after a short debate.
No seats at all and a letter of apology from the committee, which the delegation accepted quietly.
Ten seats and a vote on the party platform, which the delegation accepted only after a long debate.

questions.feedback_correct: Hamer and most of the delegation refused the compromise.

questions.text: What happened to Black voter registration in Mississippi after the Voting Rights Act of 1965?

answers.text: It stayed at about seven percent through the rest of the 1960s.
It rose from about seven percent in 1964 to about six in ten by 1967.
It fell sharply as new local rules took hold in the Delta counties.
It rose only among voters who had moved out of Mississippi to other states.

questions.feedback_correct: The Act suspended literacy tests and allowed federal examiners to register voters.

questions.text: How did the Supreme Court's 1969 decision in Alexander v. Holmes County change school desegregation?

answers.text: It ruled that districts must end segregated schools at once, which ended the excuse of delay.
It allowed districts another ten years to finish the work in a careful way.
It repealed the decision in Brown v. Board of Education and returned the question to the states.
It left the pace of change to each local school board to decide for itself.

questions.feedback_correct: The phrase "all deliberate speed" had run out.

questions.text: Robert Clark won a seat in the legislature in 1967. What did his election show?

answers.text: Black candidates had held seats in the legislature without any break at all since the year 1890.
Black Mississippians could win office once many of them could vote after the Voting Rights Act.
The legislature had been abolished and then rebuilt with new rules for membership in 1967.
The Voting Rights Act had made no real difference to who held office in Mississippi after 1965.

questions.feedback_correct: He served thirty-six years and became speaker pro tempore in 1992.

questions.text: Why did the killings at Jackson State in 1970 receive less national attention than the deaths at Kent State ten days earlier?

answers.text: No one was hurt at Jackson State, so there was very little for the national press to report on.
The officers were convicted quickly, which ended public interest in the story within a few days.
The shootings took place a full year after Kent State, when the nation had already moved on.
Reporters were not there in the same numbers, and the victims were Black students at a Black college.

questions.feedback_correct: The lesson says some chapters reach the wider public only when someone decides to tell them.

questions.text: Why did Mississippi's Constitution of 1890 divide government into three departments?

answers.text: To let the governor appoint every judge and legislator in the state without any vote.
To keep any one person or group from holding all power, with each branch limiting the others.
To make the legislature the only body allowed to make decisions for the state.
To give each county its own army and courts, free of any control from the state.

questions.feedback_correct: This is the idea of the separation of powers, explained in Federalist No. 51.

questions.text: How does Mississippi choose most of its top executive officers?

answers.text: The governor appoints all of them, with the consent of the state Senate.
The legislature chooses them from among its own members each January.
Voters elect eight statewide officers, so the governor cannot fire the others.
The Supreme Court appoints them to serve for life, subject to good behavior.

questions.feedback_correct: Because so much power goes to other elected officers, the governor has traditionally been called weaker than many governors.

questions.text: What do the five "beats" in a Mississippi county represent?

answers.text: The five courts in each county that hear all criminal and civil cases brought there.
The five districts from which members of the board of supervisors are elected.
The five tax rates that a county may set each year on homes, farms, and stores.
The five sheriffs who share the county's police work between them in turn.

questions.feedback_correct: The board sets the tax rate, builds roads and bridges, and approves the budget.

questions.text: What was one weakness critics found in the Balance Agriculture With Industry plan?

answers.text: It banned all factories from the state's small towns and sent every new job to the big cities.
It paid farmers not to plant any crop at all, which left the land empty for many years.
It tied the state to low pay and to firms that could leave, while towns still owed the bonds.
It taxed every new industry at such a high rate that no company would agree to come.

questions.feedback_correct: Supporters said the plan gave people jobs when nothing else did. Both statements held some truth.

questions.text: What did the Education Reform Act of 1982 do?

answers.text: It created public kindergartens in every district, required school attendance, and set higher standards.
It closed small rural schools in order to save money for the state treasury during the hard years.
It ended property taxes for all school districts and replaced them with a new state sales tax.
It gave control of the public schools to private companies that were chosen by the governor.

questions.feedback_correct: It was a choice to spend on the future, and it was not easy to pass.

questions.text: Which explanation for Mississippi's poverty points to the long effects of slavery and sharecropping?

answers.text: Mississippi has no rivers that could carry its goods to markets in other states.
Mississippi has had too many very large cities for a state of its size.
An economy built on cheap farm labor and a few large landowners left few towns or banks.
Mississippi never grew cotton on any large scale, so it had no farm income.

questions.feedback_correct: When cotton failed, there was no second industry to catch the people it left behind.

questions.text: Camille in 1969 was a Category 5 storm, and Katrina in 2005 was a Category 3 at landfall. Why was Katrina's surge higher in places?

answers.text: Katrina was enormous, and Mississippi lay on the stronger right side of the storm.
Katrina had stronger winds than Camille at the moment of landfall on the coast.
Camille's surge was never measured anywhere along the coast of the state.
Katrina came ashore at high tide in Alabama and pushed water west into Mississippi.

questions.feedback_correct: The surge in Mississippi reached about twenty-eight feet in places.

questions.text: Stronger building codes and higher foundations for new homes are examples of what?

answers.text: Evacuation, which moves whole towns out of the path of a storm before it arrives.
Insurance fraud, which raises the cost of coverage for every owner on the coast.
Federalism, which requires the state to rebuild every home that a storm destroys.
Mitigation, which costs owners money now and may save lives in the next storm.

questions.feedback_correct: Building higher wins no praise until the day it is needed.

questions.text: When a hurricane strikes, which level of government supplies money, supplies, and teams of workers through agencies like FEMA?

answers.text: Only the county board of supervisors, using local property tax money.
Only the local city council, using money raised from the sale of bonds.
The national government.
No level of government takes part, because private charities handle every need.

questions.feedback_correct: Local governments clear roads, the state calls out the National Guard, and the national government supplies money and supplies.

questions.text: Why did many Lebanese families in the Delta begin as peddlers?

answers.text: They were forbidden by state law to own any land or buildings in the Delta.
They came to Mississippi mainly to take jobs in the offices of local government.
They were hired by the state to run its railroads and to repair its river levees.
They had little money, so they walked farm roads with packs and later opened stores.

questions.feedback_correct: Some of the stores they began are still family businesses.

questions.text: Why did many Croatian families settle on the Mississippi Gulf Coast?

answers.text: The state gave them free land in the Delta if they would farm cotton there.
The coast reminded them of home, and fishing and canning were familiar trades.
They were invited to build the first casinos along the water in Biloxi.
They were sent there by the Army after World War II to rebuild the shipyards.

questions.feedback_correct: Croatian names are still common in coastal towns.

questions.text: Under Chief Phillip Martin, how did the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians build its economy?

answers.text: It sold the reservation to the state and moved the whole tribe to Oklahoma in the 1980s.
It depended entirely on payments from the federal government for its income, with no businesses.
It started businesses that gave jobs on the reservation, including factories and later casinos.
It leased all of the tribal land to cotton planters, who farmed it for the tribe.

questions.feedback_correct: The tribe is now among the largest employers in Mississippi.

questions.text: Why does a field recording like the Lomax recordings in Coahoma County count as a primary source, and what caution should a historian keep in mind?

answers.text: It is the final truth about the music, so no caution is needed when using it.
It lets you hear the people themselves, but someone chose whom to record and where.
Recordings are never evidence, because they are not written down on paper.
It was made by the singers alone, with no collector or machine involved at all.

questions.feedback_correct: A recording is not an accident. Someone decided what to record.

questions.text: Where is the story of the blues traditionally traced?

answers.text: To the mountains of Appalachia, from the fiddle tunes of mountain families.
To New York City, from the singers of the opera houses and concert halls.
To the Gulf Coast, from the chants that sailors sang on the old sailing ships.
To the Mississippi Delta, from field hollers, work songs, and church spirituals.

questions.feedback_correct: A single guitar, a harmonica, and a voice were enough.

questions.text: What does Elvis Presley's early sound show about Mississippi's music?

answers.text: It came only from the classical music that was taught in the state's public schools.
It mixed church music, the blues, and country, drawing on both Black and white Mississippians.
It was borrowed whole from European folk songs that early settlers brought across the sea.
It had no real connection to anything that people could hear in churches or on farms.

questions.feedback_correct: In Elvis's voice you can hear the church, the blues, and country music together.

questions.text: Which writer is correctly paired with a book discussed in Lesson 36.2?

answers.text: William Faulkner, Black Boy, a memoir of growing up in the Delta.
Eudora Welty, Native Son, a novel about a young man in Chicago.
Tennessee Williams, The Optimist's Daughter, a prize-winning novel about a family.
Richard Wright, Black Boy.

questions.feedback_correct: Wright's memoir told what it was like to grow up under Jim Crow in Mississippi.

quizzes.title: Semester Final
quizzes.description: Choose the best answer for each question. Each question stands on its own.

questions.text: The Declaration of Causes says, "For far less cause than this, our fathers separated from the Crown of England." Why compare Mississippi to the founders?

answers.text: To admit that the delegates knew very well that they were breaking the law of the land.
To ask Britain for help in a coming war against the Northern states and their armies.
To argue that the Constitution had already been repealed by the Northern states in 1860.
To present secession as a justified act in the tradition of American independence.

questions.feedback_correct: The comparison is an argument, and whether it holds up is a fair question.

questions.text: Some people say the Civil War was about "states' rights." What does the Declaration of Causes suggest about that claim?

answers.text: It defended slavery, and it argued for states' rights only when that helped.
It never mentions slavery at all and speaks only of taxes, trade, and the price of cotton.
It praises Northern state governments for protecting the liberty of their own citizens.
It argues that the federal government was too weak to collect taxes in the Southern states.

questions.feedback_correct: The document is mainly about slavery, and it says so.

questions.text: Albert Sidney Johnston was killed on the first day at Shiloh, and many historians think the battle might have gone differently had he lived. What does this show?

answers.text: Armies can never recover after they lose a commander in the middle of a large battle.
Commanders rarely matter to the outcome of any large battle fought in the open field.
Battles are decided only by the number of soldiers who are present on each side.
Outcomes can turn on what happens to one leader, so they are not fixed in advance.

questions.feedback_correct: Choices and chance, not only numbers, shaped events.

questions.text: Grant moved away from his supply base and lived partly off the land. What does that decision best show?

answers.text: A willingness to take a calculated risk and act decisively.
A habit of waiting for orders from Washington before every move.
A deep fear of losing his army in a battle he could not win.
An unwillingness to leave the river and march into the country.

questions.feedback_correct: The risk paid off at Vicksburg.

questions.text: Grant wrote his memoirs in 1885. Why should a historian compare his account with reports written in 1863?

answers.text: Memoirs always contain the exact words of every order that was given during the campaign.
Memory and hindsight can change how a writer describes what he planned and felt.
Reports from 1863 were never kept, so they are of no use to a historian today.
Grant had never been to Mississippi and had to rely on the work of other writers.

questions.feedback_correct: Comparing sources from different times helps a historian see what changed in the telling.

questions.text: What is the most important limit of using Mary Ann Loughborough's book as evidence about the siege of Vicksburg?

answers.text: It shows one family's view and leaves out many other people in the town.
It was written by someone who was not present in the town during the siege.
It cannot be used as evidence because it was published as a printed book.
It describes events from a different war that took place years before.

questions.feedback_correct: Every source has a point of view.

questions.text: What does the Confederate law excusing some men from military service show about slavery and the war effort?

answers.text: The government hoped that slavery would come to an end during the course of the war.
The government treated control of enslaved labor as part of what the war effort needed.
The government thought slavery was unimportant to the Confederate cause from the start.
The government forbade overseers from working on any large plantation in the Confederacy.

questions.feedback_correct: The law protected the supervision of enslaved workers as a wartime need.

questions.text: Suppose the law excusing some men from service had excused no one. What would most likely have happened on large plantations?

answers.text: Planters would have stopped growing crops and left their fields empty for the whole season.
Enslaved people would have been freed at once by an act of the Confederate army.
The Union army would have left Mississippi at once after the planters made their complaint.
More of the white men who supervised the work would have been drafted, leaving fewer to oversee it.

questions.feedback_correct: The exemption existed so that the plantation system could keep running during the war.

questions.text: Black men who served in the Union army often argued from their service that they had earned something. What was it?

answers.text: Ownership of the plantations where they and their families had worked.
A claim on the government and the protection of its laws as citizens.
A right to be paid wages by their former owners for past labor.
An exemption from all future taxes and from any later military service.

questions.feedback_correct: Lesson 21.2 calls a soldier's uniform a public claim to citizenship.

questions.text: Nathan Bedford Forrest beat a larger Union force at Brice's Crossroads in June 1864. What lesson did Union leaders draw?

answers.text: Cavalry could not fight well in the kind of country that is found in the state of Mississippi.
Forrest would never be seen again by the Union soldiers after such a hard fight in June.
Holding Mississippi's towns and railroads did not mean controlling the countryside.
The Union should give up its efforts in the state after the loss of so many soldiers.

questions.feedback_correct: The war in Mississippi was not over when the Union held the river.

questions.text: In December 1865 Mississippi's legislature voted not to ratify the Thirteenth Amendment. What does this suggest about how many white leaders saw emancipation?

answers.text: Many accepted it only reluctantly, as something forced on them by the war.
They had always supported it and wished to see it become the law of the whole country.
They believed it was only a state matter and not one for the national government at all.
They had never heard of it and so could not decide how they ought to vote on it.

questions.feedback_correct: The 1865 convention also wrote slavery out of the state constitution only reluctantly.

questions.text: Confederates repaired part of the railroad damage at Meridian within weeks. What does this suggest about Sherman's expedition?

answers.text: It destroyed the Confederate army completely in a single campaign.
It freed all of the enslaved people living in the state of Mississippi.
It hurt the rail network but did not end the Confederacy's ability to fight.
It ended the war in Mississippi and brought peace to the state.

questions.feedback_correct: The expedition did real damage, but its effects did not last long.

questions.text: Suppose the Senate had refused to seat Hiram Revels. What would most likely have been the effect on Reconstruction?

answers.text: The state's Republicans would have celebrated the decision as a victory for their cause.
Many would have seen the promise of equal citizenship as broken, weakening Reconstruction.
The Fifteenth Amendment would have been repealed by Congress within the following year.
Mississippi would have been readmitted to the Union much sooner than had been planned.

questions.feedback_correct: His seating was a test of whether the new order would be honored.

questions.text: Why was a Mississippi senator a useful voice for Black citizens in the South?

answers.text: He could veto any bill that came before the Congress of the United States and its committees.
He could command federal troops and send them to any county in the state that he chose.
He could speak in the Senate and ask Washington for protection, though he could not make law alone.
He could rewrite the state's laws by himself by a decision made under the powers of his office.

questions.feedback_correct: A senator has a platform where national lawmakers must hear him.

questions.text: Suppose the Constitution of 1868 had not created public schools. What would most likely have been true for most Black children?

answers.text: They would have attended the very same schools in any case, with no change in their chances.
They would have had far fewer chances to attend school, since few families could pay.
They would have gone on to college in large numbers by way of the army's training schools.
They would have been taught by soldiers of the Union army in camps set up in each county.

questions.feedback_correct: Most freed families had little money, so public schools were their best path to learning.

questions.text: What did the Enforcement Acts of 1870 and 1871 make a federal crime?

answers.text: Joining the Republican Party in a county where it was weak.
Selling cotton on credit to a family that could not pay.
Running for office in a state without a license from the governor.
Using force or threats to stop a citizen from voting.

questions.feedback_correct: They also let the president use the army against groups that held whole counties in fear.

questions.text: Why did Democrats treat James Alcorn, a wealthy planter who joined the Republicans, as a traitor?

answers.text: He was a Northerner who had come South after the war to seek power.
He was a Union general who stayed in Mississippi after the war ended.
He was a scalawag, a white Southerner who joined the Republican Party.
He was a Black delegate to the state constitutional convention of 1868.

questions.feedback_correct: Alcorn and Ames became rivals, and moderate whites turned against the Republican government.

questions.text: After the Clinton massacre in September 1875, what answer did Governor Ames receive when he asked Washington for troops?

answers.text: Troops were sent within a few days to protect the voters at the polls in the Delta counties.
Congress voted to make Mississippi a territory under direct rule by the federal government.
The president resigned in protest and left the whole matter to his successor to settle later.
The public was tired of yearly outbreaks in the South, and Mississippi should handle its own affairs.

questions.feedback_correct: Left without help, Ames made a deal that the Democrats did not keep.

questions.text: A Senate committee led by George Boutwell collected testimony about the 1875 election in 1876. What did Congress do?

answers.text: It overturned the election results and ordered a new vote in the state.
It did not act to protect Mississippi's voters.
It sent troops at once to guard the polls in every county.
It expelled Senator Bruce for speaking against the election.

questions.feedback_correct: Some call the result an abandonment of Reconstruction.

questions.text: The 1890 convention required voters to pay a two-dollar poll tax. Why did this hit many tenant farmers hardest?

answers.text: The tax applied only to Black voters and to no one else in the state.
The tax was refunded to every voter after the election was over.
The tax applied only to landowners, so tenants were not affected.
Tenants rarely saw cash, so even a small sum could keep them from voting.

questions.feedback_correct: A poll tax falls hardest on those with little cash.

questions.text: Only one of the 134 delegates at the 1890 convention was Black. What does that show?

answers.text: Black delegates had chosen not to attend the convention that was held in Jackson that year.
Black delegates were a majority at the convention and wrote the new rules for the state.
Black Mississippians, a majority of the state's people, had almost no voice in writing the rules.
The convention was held in secret and its members' names were never made known to the public.

questions.feedback_correct: Isaiah Montgomery was the only Black delegate.

questions.text: Mississippi was the first state to rewrite its constitution to limit the vote in this way. What followed?

answers.text: Other Southern states copied its ideas over the next few years.
Federal courts ended the practice in the state within a year.
Mississippi repealed the voting rules in 1892 after many protests.
No other state followed its example, and the idea was soon dropped.

questions.feedback_correct: Williams v. Mississippi in 1898 made it easier for other states to copy it.

questions.text: How did Ida B. Wells investigate lynchings?

answers.text: She relied on rumor and local gossip told to her by friends who lived in Memphis town.
She traveled, gathered facts from newspapers and interviews, and printed names and dates.
She wrote works of fiction based on what she had heard from other people in her travels.
She avoided the cases themselves and wrote only her own opinions about what she had heard.

questions.feedback_correct: She believed the facts, shown plainly, were the strongest weapon a citizen had.

questions.text: Mississippi's Democrats made their primary open only to white voters. Why did that matter?

answers.text: It gave Republicans more seats in the legislature than they had held before the change.
It required approval from the federal courts before each election could take place.
It ended the poll tax and the literacy test for all voters in every county of the state.
With one party holding nearly every office, the real choice was made in the primary.

questions.feedback_correct: The Constitution of 1890 and the party primary worked together.

questions.text: Alcorn University, opened in 1871, was notable for what reason?

answers.text: It was the nation's first college for women of any race.
It was the nation's first land-grant college for Black students.
It was the first law school opened in the South after the war.
It was the first private academy built by the Citizens' Council.

questions.feedback_correct: Church and missionary groups also founded Tougaloo, Rust, and Jackson State.

questions.text: What caused the crevasse at Mounds Landing in April 1927?

answers.text: A dam upriver was destroyed by soldiers of the Army Corps of Engineers.
An earthquake cracked the riverbank at the edge of the Delta.
A levee in Bolivar County gave way under the rising river.
A steamboat rammed the levee in the dark and opened a hole.

questions.feedback_correct: Water poured through and spread across the Delta.

questions.text: In 1927 President Coolidge was reluctant to spend federal money on flood victims. Who carried much of the response?

answers.text: The Red Cross and local leaders.
The Army alone, using money from the federal budget.
Congress, which passed a large relief law in the first week.
The Weather Bureau, which ran the camps along the levees.

questions.feedback_correct: After the disaster, Congress decided that a flood crossing many states was a national problem.

questions.text: Which Mississippi city was the first to receive electricity from the Tennessee Valley Authority, in 1934?

answers.text: Jackson, the state capital and its largest city.
Biloxi, on the Gulf Coast near the shipyards.
Tupelo.
Natchez, the old river town on the bluffs.

questions.feedback_correct: The New Deal brought changes that people could see.

questions.text: In 1946 Medgar Evers and his brother Charles were turned away when they tried to vote in Decatur. What had Medgar just done?

answers.text: He had finished his degree at the law school at Ole Miss.
He had run for a county office and lost by a few votes.
He had founded the first chapter of the NAACP in the state.
He had come home from Army service in Europe in World War II.

questions.feedback_correct: He had fought overseas for a country that would not let him vote at home.

questions.text: Moses Wright pointed at the two men in court in 1955. Why was that an act of great courage?

answers.text: He was a paid witness for the government who had been given police protection by the court.
He was an older Black sharecropper naming white men at a time when that risked his life.
The jury had ordered him to point at the men in the courtroom, and he did as he was told.
He had already left the state and was safe from any harm by the time the trial began.

questions.feedback_correct: After the trial, Wright left Mississippi.

questions.text: The Reverend George Lee refused to take his name off the voting rolls. Why?

answers.text: He saw registration as a duty and urged others to register.
He did not know about the order that was given to him by the Council.
He was running for office that year and needed every vote he could get.
He had been paid by the county to keep his name on the rolls.

questions.feedback_correct: He was shot and killed on May 7, 1955.

questions.text: Hodding Carter Jr. criticized the Citizens' Council. What happened to him?

answers.text: He was elected governor on the strength of his editorials against the Council.
He faced boycotts, but he kept writing.
He was sent to prison for printing the names of the Council's members.
He joined the Council and wrote in praise of its work.

questions.feedback_correct: Not every white Mississippian agreed with the Council, but few spoke out.

questions.text: Justice Hugo Black refused to block the order admitting James Meredith. Why did that matter?

answers.text: It ended the case in Governor Barnett's favor and sent Meredith home.
It moved the case to a state court where the governor could hear it.
It canceled the order until the following year so that tempers could cool.
It made the law clear: Meredith had a right to attend, and the order stood.

questions.feedback_correct: The law was now clear, but state officials still would not accept it.

questions.text: On the night of September 30, 1962, what did the state highway patrol do at Oxford?

answers.text: It arrested the rioters near the Lyceum and restored order by midnight.
It escorted Meredith to his first class in the morning.
It withdrew, leaving the marshals to defend the campus alone.
It fired tear gas at the marshals who were holding the campus.

questions.feedback_correct: More than 150 marshals were hurt before army soldiers arrived.

questions.text: Byron De La Beckwith was convicted in 1994. What helped bring about the new prosecution?

answers.text: Reports on Sovereignty Commission files showed it had helped check jurors, and Myrlie Evers kept working.
A confession that Beckwith made to a minister in 1965 and later repeated to a reporter.
A new federal law passed in 1968 that reopened every unsolved case from the civil rights years.
A Supreme Court order issued in 1970 that overturned the results of his first two trials.

questions.feedback_correct: The conviction came nearly thirty-one years after the killing.

questions.text: Why did Bob Moses and his coworkers move from McComb north into the Delta?

answers.text: McComb had no churches left in which they could hold their meetings.
Black residents were the majority there and the need was greatest.
The Delta had no Klan, so the work there would be perfectly safe.
A federal court ordered them to leave McComb and move north at once.

questions.feedback_correct: They did not leave Mississippi after Herbert Lee was killed.

questions.text: Fannie Lou Hamer tried to register in Indianola in 1962. What happened when she returned to the plantation?

answers.text: The owner told her to withdraw her application or leave, and she left.
She was given a raise for her courage and a house of her own.
She was elected to lead the other workers on the plantation.
She was arrested at the gate by federal agents sent from Jackson.

questions.feedback_correct: Days later, shots were fired into a house where she was staying.

questions.text: Freedom Schools met in churches and on porches. What did they teach?

answers.text: Only Bible study, with no questions allowed from the students.
Reading, history, and how government works, and they welcomed questions.
Only farming methods, taught by the owners of large plantations.
Only typing and bookkeeping, for jobs in the offices of Northern cities.

questions.feedback_correct: Many students left convinced that they could help shape their state.

questions.text: In 1967 a federal court convicted seven men in the Neshoba case. Of what crime?

answers.text: Murder under the laws of the state of Mississippi.
Treason against the United States and its government.
The burning of a church and nothing else at all.
Conspiracy to violate the victims' civil rights.

questions.feedback_correct: The state did not bring murder charges. Edgar Ray Killen was convicted of manslaughter in 2005.

questions.text: What happened to James Meredith at the start of his 1966 march from Memphis to Jackson?

answers.text: He was shot and wounded near Hernando, and other leaders finished the march.
He was arrested in Memphis and held for a week before he was set free again.
He gave up in Canton and went home to rest after the long walk in the heat.
He was elected to Congress along the way by the people he met on the road.

questions.feedback_correct: About fifteen thousand people marched into Jackson on June 26.

questions.text: In 1992 the Supreme Court ruled in the Ayers case that Mississippi had not done enough to end what?

answers.text: The mixing of high schools and the busing of children across towns.
The operation of Jackson State College as a public university.
The old system that funded white universities more than Black ones.
The funding of private academies out of the state's public money.

questions.feedback_correct: Years later the state agreed to spend a large sum on its historically Black colleges.

questions.text: After leaving office, Governor William Winter spent much of his life working on what?

answers.text: Expanding the Citizens' Council to every state in the Deep South in the 1980s.
Moving the state capital from the city of Jackson to a new site in the Delta.
Restoring the Sovereignty Commission and its files to full use by the state.
Racial reconciliation, including a center at the University of Mississippi.

questions.feedback_correct: Reconciliation means telling the truth about what happened and working together to do better.

questions.text: A governor may veto a bill. How can the Mississippi legislature override a veto?

answers.text: By a simple majority vote in only one of the two houses.
By a two-thirds vote in each house.
By a vote of the state Supreme Court on the bill's merits.
By a decision of the lieutenant governor made on his own.

questions.feedback_correct: The governor may also veto particular items in money bills.

questions.text: What is judicial review?

answers.text: The governor's power to remove judges from office at any time during their terms.
A review of the voter rolls that the legislature carries out each year in every county.
A court's power to decide that a law breaks the constitution and to refuse to enforce it.
A county board's power to set the property tax rate that applies in its own district.

questions.feedback_correct: It is a check on the legislature and on the governor.

questions.text: Why is the circuit clerk of a county especially important to citizens?

answers.text: The clerk collects the property taxes owed by every home and farm.
The clerk keeps court records and is in charge of voter registration.
The clerk keeps order in the county and runs the county jail.
The clerk sets the county tax rate and votes on the budget.

questions.feedback_correct: Who held this office mattered a great deal during the fight over the ballot.

questions.text: Why does Mississippi law require most meetings of public boards to be open to the public?

answers.text: Open meetings raise money for the county through the sale of seats to the public.
Federal courts demand open meetings for every public board in every state of the country.
Open meetings are a way to train new sheriffs and deputies for their future work.
A free people must be able to see how its money is spent and how decisions are made.

questions.feedback_correct: A meeting no one attends is a meeting where only insiders have a say.

questions.text: What did the boll weevil do to Mississippi farms in the early 1900s?

answers.text: In some years it ruined much of the cotton crop.
It doubled the price of cotton by making the crop scarce.
It ended sharecropping across the whole state at one stroke.
It harmed only the fish that were raised along the Gulf Coast.

questions.feedback_correct: The weevil and the flood were accidents of nature that piled on top of one another.

questions.text: Nissan opened a plant at Canton in 2003 and Toyota one at Blue Springs in 2011. How is the state's approach like the earlier BAWI plan?

answers.text: Both banned unions from the plants in order to keep wages low.
Both used incentives to attract companies.
Both depended on the state's cotton crop for their raw materials.
Both closed public schools in order to pay for the new factories.

questions.feedback_correct: It is the same idea in a modern form.

questions.text: Catfish farming began in the Delta in the 1960s. Why did the region suit it?

answers.text: The land is flat, water is plentiful, and the clay soil holds water well.
The weather is very cold in winter and freezes the ponds solid for months at a time.
The hills are rocky and steep and drain the rain water quickly away from the fields.
The rivers carry salt water from the Gulf far up into the heart of the Delta region.

questions.feedback_correct: Humphreys County and its seat, Belzoni, took the name Catfish Capital of the World.

questions.text: Many people stayed through the night of Camille. Why?

answers.text: Leaving the coast was against the law during the hurricane season, so families stayed in place.
No storm warnings had ever been issued by any government agency that was in charge of such things.
Soldiers had closed every road that led away from the coast, so families could not leave.
Earlier storms had turned away, warnings were not always believed, and moving a family is hard.

questions.feedback_correct: Others had no car or nowhere to go.

questions.text: After Katrina, many homeowners argued with their insurers. About what?

answers.text: Whether the storm was truly a hurricane or only a very strong gale that had passed over.
Whether the house had been located in the state of Alabama or in the state of Mississippi.
Whether wind, which was covered, or rising water, which was not, had destroyed the house.
Whether the insurance company had ever sold any insurance to the family before the storm.

questions.feedback_correct: A family's money and trust could be tested twice, first by the storm and then by the paperwork.

questions.text: After Katrina, why did the legislature allow casinos to be built on land close to the water?

answers.text: So that casinos would not be washed away on barges again.
To avoid paying any state tax on the new buildings.
Because a federal order required them to build on land.
To make room for a new port on the open water.

questions.feedback_correct: Larger resorts followed.

questions.text: Why were Chinese Mississippians often treated as outsiders by both white and Black Mississippians under Jim Crow?

answers.text: Chinese law forbade families from mixing with their neighbors once they came to Mississippi.
They refused to work in any local business that was owned by other people in the town.
The system sorted people into two groups and had no clear place for a Chinese family.
They were not allowed by the state to become citizens of the United States of any kind.

questions.feedback_correct: Chinese Mississippians made their own way through family businesses, churches, and close ties.

questions.text: What did the Choctaw constitution of 1975 set up?

answers.text: A state senate and a house of representatives for the tribe.
A county board of supervisors with five elected members.
A federal agency to run the reservation from Washington.
A tribal council, an elected chief, and courts.

questions.feedback_correct: It also describes the rights and duties of tribal members.

questions.text: What did the arrests of nearly seven hundred workers at central Mississippi poultry plants in 2019 show?

answers.text: How deeply some towns depended on immigrant workers, and that the event divided public opinion.
That every poultry worker in the state was a citizen who held all of the proper papers.
That the poultry plants had closed for good after the arrests and never opened again.
That the state had no poultry industry to speak of at the time of the arrests.

questions.feedback_correct: Some said the law had to be enforced, and others said families were being torn apart.

questions.text: W. C. Handy said he first heard the blues in 1903 at the train station in Tutwiler. Why does the lesson say his story should be read with care?

answers.text: Handy never lived in Mississippi and had never been to the town of Tutwiler in his life.
The story has been proved false by every historian who has studied the question carefully.
Like any story told by one person, it reflects his own memory, though it points to something real.
Handy was a small child when the event is said to have happened, so he could not recall it.

questions.feedback_correct: The sound was already in the Delta, waiting to be noticed.

questions.text: The lesson says the legend that Robert Johnson sold his soul at a crossroads should be doubted. Why?

answers.text: No record supports it.
He lived to a very old age and never spoke of such a thing.
He never learned to play the guitar and was only a singer.
He made no recordings at all, so little is known about him.

questions.feedback_correct: He left a few recordings that later artists studied for decades.

questions.text: What does the lesson mean when it says beauty and goodness are connected but not the same?

answers.text: Beautiful art is always good in its effects on the people who see it or hear it in any age.
Good people cannot make art, because goodness takes up all of the time that a person has.
A beautiful song does not make a society just, and an unjust society cannot erase its beauty.
Justice in a state depends on how much art the people of that state have made over time.

questions.feedback_correct: Part of the work of history is to hold both facts without letting one cancel the other.

How confident do you feel about this module's material?

Name one virtue the people in this module needed, and explain your choice with one example from the module.

discussions.title: Module 19 Discussion: Fifteen Said No: Was Secession Inevitable?
discussions.html:
Fifteen delegates voted against secession, and many Mississippians wanted to wait. Choose one claim and defend it with evidence from this module's sources.

Claim A: By January 1861, secession in Mississippi could no longer have been stopped.

Claim B: Secession was a choice, and Mississippi's leaders could have chosen differently.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use at least one detail from Primary Source 19.1 or Primary Source 19.2, and one detail from Lesson 19.1 or Lesson 19.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 20 Discussion: Could Vicksburg Have Held?
discussions.html:
Historians still argue about whether Vicksburg could have held. Choose the explanation you find strongest and defend it.

Option A: Pemberton should have given up the city while he still had an army to save.

Option B: Johnston should have attacked Grant from behind.

Option C: The Confederacy simply did not have the men and supplies to defend two fronts at once.

Use one detail from Lesson 20.1 or Lesson 20.2, and one detail from either Grant's memoir (Primary Source 20.1) or Loughborough's book (Primary Source 20.2). Then reply to one classmate who chose a different option. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 21 Discussion: Whose War Was It?
discussions.html:
The war reached every kind of Mississippian, but not in the same way. Choose one group and make a claim about what the war asked of them.

Group A: poor white farm families.

Group B: women running farms and households.

Group C: enslaved Mississippians.

Group D: Black men who joined the Union army.

State your claim, then explain why. Use one detail from Lesson 21.1 or Lesson 21.2, and one detail from Primary Source 21.1 or Primary Source 21.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose a different group. Is the war more "theirs" than yours, or less? Explain your thinking.

discussions.title: Module 22 Discussion: Was Mississippi's 1865 Answer a Choice or an Accident?
discussions.html:
Mississippi's Black Code passed through a legislature in regular session, a governor signed it, and courts enforced it. Yet Lesson 22.2 also says that Johnson's quick plan and the lack of Black voters made harsh laws easier to pass. Choose one claim and defend it.

Claim A: The Black Codes were mostly a choice, because men voted for them and other choices were possible.

Claim B: The Black Codes were mostly the result of circumstances, because the plan Johnson set up made them likely.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 22.2 and one detail from Lesson 22.1 or Lesson 22.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 23 Discussion: Why Did Revels Matter?
discussions.html:
Hiram Revels held his Senate seat for about a year and could not change the laws by himself. Was he more important as a symbol or as a source of power? Choose one and defend it.

Claim A: Revels mattered mainly as a symbol of what citizenship could look like.

Claim B: Revels mattered mainly because of the power his office gave him, or the power others held in offices like his, such as local sheriffs and school officials.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 23.1 or Primary Source 23.2, and one detail from Lesson 23.1 or Lesson 23.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 24 Discussion: Was Reconstruction Overthrown or Abandoned?
discussions.html:
Lesson 24.2 says some historians call the end of Reconstruction in Mississippi an overthrow, and others call it an abandonment. Choose one word and defend it.

Claim A: Reconstruction in Mississippi was overthrown, mainly by Mississippians who used force against their neighbors.

Claim B: Reconstruction in Mississippi was abandoned, mainly by a federal government that could have protected voters and chose not to.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 24.1 or Primary Source 24.2, and one detail from Lesson 24.1 or Lesson 24.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 25 Discussion: Montgomery's Vote: Prudence or Surrender?
discussions.html:
At the 1890 convention, Isaiah Montgomery, the only Black delegate, voted for rules that would shrink the Black vote. He argued that peace was worth the price. Historians still disagree about his choice. Choose one claim and defend it.

Claim A: Montgomery's vote was prudent, because he faced a plan he could not stop and hoped to protect his people from worse violence.

Claim B: Montgomery's vote was a surrender, because it gave a Black face to a plan designed to shut his own people out.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 25.1 or Primary Source 25.2, and one detail from Lesson 25.1 or Lesson 25.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 26 Discussion: Why Did Wells Leave, and Why Did Others Stay?
discussions.html:
Ida B. Wells left Mississippi, and her leaving saved her life and made her national work possible. Many other Black Mississippians stayed, and their staying built churches, schools, and communities that lasted. Lesson 26.2 says that staying was not the weaker choice and leaving was not the braver one. Choose one claim and defend it.

Claim A: Leaving did more to serve Black Mississippians, because it gave people safety, better pay, and a voice that could not be silenced.

Claim B: Staying did more to serve Black Mississippians, because it kept families, land, and institutions in the state and built a base for later change.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 26.1 or Primary Source 26.2, and one detail from Lesson 26.1 or Lesson 26.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 27 Discussion: What Does a State Owe the People It Moves by Force?
discussions.html:
Lesson 27.2 points out that in 1927 refugees were held in camps and made to work, in the 1930s tenants were pushed off the land, and in the 1940s young men were drafted. Each group was moved, but under very different rules. Choose one claim and defend it.

Claim A: A state owes the same basic care to anyone it moves, whether by a draft, a relief camp, or an eviction.

Claim B: What a state owes depends on whether the person consented and what the state asked in return, so a soldier is owed more than a flood refugee.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 27.1 or Primary Source 27.2, and one detail from Lesson 27.1 or Lesson 27.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 28 Discussion: Why Did Mississippi Choose Defiance?
discussions.html:
Lesson 28.1 says that Mississippi's answer to Brown was "a choice, not a fate." Historians still ask how free those leaders really were. Choose one claim and defend it.

Claim A: Mississippi's defiance was mainly a choice, because its leaders had other options, such as obeying and adjusting, and turned them down.

Claim B: Mississippi's defiance was mainly the result of pressures, such as the state's large Black population, its cotton economy, and the memory of Reconstruction, that made another answer unlikely.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 28.1 or Primary Source 28.2, and one detail from Lesson 28.1 or Lesson 28.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 29 Discussion: Barnett or Kennedy: Who Was Right About Authority?
discussions.html:
In September 1962, Governor Ross Barnett said schools were a state matter under the Tenth Amendment. President Kennedy said federal law was supreme and a court order had to be carried out. Choose one claim and defend it as an argument about authority.

Claim A: When a state and the national government disagree about matters like schools, the state should have the last word.

Claim B: When a state and the national government disagree, federal law and federal court orders must win.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 29.1 or Primary Source 29.2, and one detail from Lesson 29.1 or Lesson 29.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short. Remember whose right was at the center of the dispute.

discussions.title: Module 30 Discussion: Was Atlantic City a Failure or a Beginning?
discussions.html:
The Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party asked to be seated in 1964 and was offered two at-large seats, which it refused. Lesson 30.2 says some called this a betrayal and others said the testimony changed the debate. Choose one claim and defend it.

Claim A: The challenge at Atlantic City was mainly a failure, because the delegates did not win what they came for.

Claim B: The challenge at Atlantic City was mainly a beginning, because the testimony reached millions and the rules changed because they asked.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 30.1 or Primary Source 30.2, and one detail from Lesson 30.1 or Lesson 30.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 31 Discussion: What Was the Movement's Greatest Achievement?
discussions.html:
Lesson 31.2 asks whether Mississippi became an open state. Choose the change you think mattered most and defend it.

Claim A: The greatest achievement was political: the vote, and the first Black officeholders in nearly a century.

Claim B: The greatest achievement was in everyday life: desegregated schools, colleges, and public places that opened to everyone.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 31.1 or Primary Source 31.2, and one detail from Lesson 31.1 or Lesson 31.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 32 Discussion: Is Mississippi's Constitution a Good Constitution?
discussions.html:
Mississippi divides power among three branches, elects eight statewide officers, and spreads local power across 82 counties. Choose one claim about this design and defend it.

Claim A: Mississippi's constitution is mostly a good one, because it divides power widely and keeps any one person from controlling the state.

Claim B: Mississippi's constitution is mostly a poor one, because no one is clearly in charge, and because it was written in 1890 to shut many citizens out.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 32.1 or Primary Source 32.2, and one detail from Lesson 32.1 or Lesson 32.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 33 Discussion: What Would Mississippi Look Like Without the 1890 Constitution?
discussions.html:
Lesson 33.2 says Mississippi's poverty has several causes, and it asks you to imagine the state without the Constitution of 1890. Choose one claim and defend it.

Claim A: Without the 1890 Constitution, Mississippi would probably be richer and more equal today, because Black citizens would have kept the vote and a voice in school spending.

Claim B: Without the 1890 Constitution, Mississippi would probably still be poor, because cotton dependence, distance from big cities, and low incomes had other causes.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 33.1 or Primary Source 33.2, and one detail from Lesson 33.1 or Lesson 33.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 34 Discussion: Should Mississippians Rebuild on the Coast?
discussions.html:
Lesson 34.2 sets two goods against each other: the liberty of owners to use their own land, and the common good, which includes safety and the fair use of public money. Choose one claim and defend it.

Claim A: The coast should be rebuilt where it stood, because families, jobs, and history are there and owners have a right to their land.

Claim B: Rebuilding on the lowest ground should be limited, because the next storm will bring the same loss and the public pays to insure and repair it.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 34.1 or Primary Source 34.2, and one detail from Lesson 34.1 or Lesson 34.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 35 Discussion: What Does It Take to Belong to Mississippi?
discussions.html:
Lesson 35.2 says belonging has more than one meaning: legal, social, and the belonging of a people who were here before the state. Choose one claim and defend it.

Claim A: Belonging mainly depends on law: citizenship, equal treatment, and the rights that come with them.

Claim B: Belonging mainly depends on community: how neighbors treat a person day after day.

State which claim you find stronger, then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 35.1 or Primary Source 35.2, and one detail from Lesson 35.1 or Lesson 35.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose the other claim. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.

discussions.title: Module 36 Discussion: Why Mississippi?
discussions.html:
This course began with secession and ends with music, books, and art. Lesson 36.2 asks why a state so troubled has mattered so much. Choose the answer you find strongest, or write your own, and defend it.

Claim A: Mississippi matters because it is where the great questions of American life, about freedom, justice, poverty, belonging, and beauty, were asked in their hardest forms.

Claim B: Mississippi matters most for what it gave the nation and the world in music, writing, and art, often from people the state treated badly.

State which claim you find stronger (or write your own answer), then explain why. Use one detail from Primary Source 36.1 or Primary Source 36.2, and one detail from Lesson 36.1 or Lesson 36.2. Then reply to one classmate who chose a different answer. Do you find their reasoning persuasive? If not, say where it falls short.
